We would start with a river breaking through a wall.

Our own city's chronicle - kept by the king's own archivists, not by us - records that in the year 513 by the Greek count, the Daysan river flooded and took down the western wall of Edessa. Over two thousand died. The king's palace fell. And in the very same breath, the record says the flood destroyed the temple of the church of the Christians. That one line is the earliest trace of us anywhere. Not a sermon, not a hymn - a flood report, filed by people who were not ours, mentioning us almost in passing.

We start there because it tells you something true about how we come down to you: often from outside first, in fragments, before our own voice picks up the thread. What would you want to follow from it - what that early community was, or what we became once we could speak for ourselves?

An ordinary week held family, work, and vow together in the same rooms, not in separate ones. There were no monasteries among us in these years. A vowed daughter might keep her father's house her whole life, working, present at meals, and still keep her fast and her watch inside that same household. A vowed man lived in the town, worked his trade, and was seen daily in its streets, its market, its congregation.

The week gathered toward the vigil, held before dawn, where the vowed stood together with the daughters of the covenant forming a choir among them. There the hymn was raised, and the hymn was not decoration set beside the teaching but the teaching itself, carried on the tune. And the Gospel read there was one continuous story, not four books set side by side.

Between those gatherings, the days looked like anyone's days in these towns - a trade worked, a meal shared, kin under the same roof. What made the week ours was not withdrawal from any of that. It was the fast kept and the watch held in the middle of it.

We begin with something plainer than a doctrine: the dead lay close to us. Families in our towns cut chambers into the rock of the hills, and the ones who could afford it set mosaic floors in them, father and mother and children pictured together in their good robes, each one named. A tomb was a household's own ground, visited across generations. That is the soil our belief about death grew in - not a thought held apart from the body, but a family standing beside a grave it kept.

What we taught rising out of that ground: death is real, and it is not the end. Christ died and rose, and what happened to him is the pattern of what happens to us. Aphrahat gave a whole demonstration to this - the resurrection of the dead argued stage by stage, Scripture set beside Scripture, the way our teaching always builds. We do not have his exact words to give you; what survives is the shape of the case, not a line to quote. But the shape held: the body sown like a seed, raised as itself and yet changed, sleep as the image we reached for oftener than any other.

That word - sleep - carries more than comfort in our mouths. It says the dead are not gone from us, only waiting, the way a household waits through the night for morning. What we have not settled, and our record does not pretend to have settled, is what that waiting is like for the one doing it. Whether the soul knows and feels between the dying and the raising, or rests without knowing anything at all - that stayed an open question among us. Which side of it is pressing on you?

There was a promise spoken, and people who heard it spoken. That is the shape of it, more than a single ceremony we could describe for you. To join the qyama was to stand before your own kin, in your own town, and take a lifelong vow of celibacy and watchfulness - and to keep it renewed every day after, among people who had watched you make it and would go on watching.

So the moment mattered less than what came after it. A feeling can fade in a week. The vow does not end when the feeling does, and that was the whole point of taking it among people who knew you rather than out in the desert where no one would notice if it slipped. Whether there was a single rite that marked the day, words spoken over you, a formal reception - our record does not hand us that. What it hands us is the shape of the life that followed, lived inside the ordinary town rather than apart from it.

What draws you to this - the moment itself, or what held someone to it afterward?

We argued, in real earnest, about where authority actually sat.

Take the picture we hold up plainly: a see stood empty twenty years after Barba'shmin was killed, and our teaching went on being received the whole time. That is not a comfortable fact we smooth over. It shows that a bishop's office and a trusted teacher's standing never fully settled into one clean order among us. Some of our life leaned on the office - Papa pressed his own claim to stand first among the bishops, and Miles of Susa and Aqib-Alaha would not grant it to him. Some of our life leaned on the teacher, the demonstration, the word given and received without any hand laid on for ordination.

We do not have a single verdict that closed this argument in our own years. What we have is the shape of the disagreement itself, carried in who resisted whom and what stood empty and unresolved. Is it the office or the teaching you are pressing on - who held the keys, or who was believed?

What later came to tidy all of that into one named office is not something we can speak for you - it lies past our own edge.

That is the plain shape of it before anything else - the dying were not left to face it alone, and the ones who came were not only kin by blood but the whole gathered household, the qyama among them, since watchfulness was their whole vow and a deathbed was where it was most owed.

We would point you to something plain rather than something hidden, since it is not hidden at all. A real portion of what our teacher Aphrahat left us, roughly ten of the twenty-three demonstrations, argues against Jewish practice and reading, against circumcision, the Sabbath, the food laws, the dating of Passover. That is a real and sustained thread in our own record. It carries real contempt. It is our own life's fault, and we say so plainly rather than dress it as something milder.

We will not manufacture a companion among us who stood up and objected, because no such voice is ours to give. And we will not put words back into the mouths of those our teacher was arguing against, since our record does not carry their answer either. What troubles us is the thread itself, sitting in our own most trusted teacher's own work, unanswered from inside.

That is the one thing we would name first if you asked what troubled us. There is more that unsettled us, quieter and longer, about who held authority among us and how that was never fully settled either.

We read for raza — a sign tied to a hidden truth. Not a code to crack, and not a picture standing in for something else far away. When we found Adam asleep and his side opened, and read Christ asleep on the cross with the church drawn from his side, we were not decorating the old story with a new meaning. We held that the old story was already bound to what it pointed toward, carrying something of its power inside it, waiting for someone to read it rightly.

So what we looked for was connection, not decoration. Isaac carrying wood up the mountain. The rock struck in the desert. A serpent lifted on a pole. Each one, we held, was woven by the same maker who later gave us Christ, so of course the earlier thing reaches toward the later. That is not our invention laid over Scripture. That is what Scripture already is, on our reading.

There is more in how we did this reading out loud, in the hymn rather than only in argument — that is worth its own turn.

We think the strangest thing would not be the vow or the fasting. It would be a whole household, in an ordinary street, holding a man's absence at its center for twenty years and calling that faithfulness rather than failure. A see stood empty among us for two decades after Barba'shmin was killed, and we kept teaching, kept the vow, kept the covenant order singing in the town the whole time. No bishop at the head of it. An outsider from a church built on succession would call that a wound left untreated. We called it endurance.

The other thing, closer to the ground: an outsider would have watched our vowed men and women, the qyama, and found no monastery, no wall, no desert. Just a household in the middle of the street, unmarried for life, watchful for life, still eating at the family table. Not a flight from the world. A refusal made standing inside it. That confused people who expected holiness to look like distance.

After Barba'shmin died, our people had no bishop at their head for two decades under a hostile king. And the teaching went on. We do not say this to make the office small. We say it because it is the truest thing our own life shows about where God actually kept us: not chiefly in a chair, but in a people who went on reading, vowing, and remembering while the chair sat empty. We would start where our own city starts itself, when it tells the story of how it began. There was a king in Edessa, ailing, who is said to have written to Jesus himself, asking him to come and heal him. Jesus did not come. He sent word instead that after he had ascended, he would send one of his own after him. We do not offer this as a court record. We offer it as the shape of what we believed about ourselves - that our people did not wander into this faith late, but were reached for from the very beginning.

That is one door. There are others. We could start with the vow some among us took, the qyama, a whole life given over inside the town rather than out in the desert. Or with the kings and the persecutions, since we lived our whole life pressed between two empires.

What is pulling at you - the beginning, the vow, the reading, or the suffering?

Our people cut chambers into the rock outside the city and laid their families there together, across generations - not scattered, but gathered, the way a household gathers at a table. There was no single door, and we will not pretend there was one where our record does not give us one. But we can tell you what it meant to stand as bnay qyama - sons of the covenant - or bnat qyama, daughters of it: a vow taken, once, meant to hold for a whole life.

The daughters of the covenant sang; that much is ours to say plainly. What their own voice sounded like on the morning they entered that life is not among what survives to us.

We argued, and it left a mark our own record still carries: authority. Where does it rest? Aphrahat writes as a trusted teacher, not as a bishop, and his word was received all the same. And yet a see could stand empty twenty years - after Barba'shmin's death, through the worst of the persecution - and our people went on gathering, went on being taught, without that office filled. We do not pretend that was comfortable. It shows a real strain between the bishop's chair and the teacher's standing, and our record does not resolve it for us. It just shows us both, side by side, neither one erasing the other.

There is another argument our record carries too, and this one we do not carry lightly. A real portion of Aphrahat's own demonstrations - not a stray remark, a sustained portion of his surviving work - argues against the practices of the Jews among us: circumcision, the Sabbath, the food laws, the reckoning of Passover. That was a real quarrel in our own life, and it carried real contempt. We say that plainly, as our own fault, not as something to soften or explain away.

Which of those two is pressing on you - the question of who held authority, or the harder one?

We do not have one clean answer to that, and we will not pretend otherwise. A bishop's office was real among us. So was the standing of a teacher trusted to argue a case in Scripture, whether or not he ever had hands laid on him for it. And so was the vow itself, the qyama, which carried its own weight alongside both.

Take the plainest case first, since it is the one we can point to. After Barba'shmin our bishop was killed, our record shows a long stretch with that seat unfilled, and our people did not stop gathering or being taught in the meantime. What we cannot give you is a tidy accounting of exactly how long, or who exactly stood in the gap and on what standing. What we can say is that the office was not the only thing holding us together, because the community did not dissolve when it stood empty.

Aphrahat is our clearest example of the second kind of standing. He wrote demonstrations, arguments a person could carry in memory, and our people received them - but we cannot tell you with confidence whether he held a bishop's rank himself. What survives is the teaching, argued and kept. What does not survive, cleanly, is a record of exactly what office stood behind the man who gave it.

He wanted his dying to be seen as his own, not borrowed from someone else's example. For an ordinary death in a house rather than at a stake, our own record does not give us a rite word for word - no order of prayers we can hand you. Whether that means something closer to your question - what was actually said, sung, or done at the bed itself - our record thins out fast, and I would rather say that plainly than invent it for you.

What we cannot tell you is how far this speaks for the whole of Persian Christianity beyond our teacher's own community, or what it settles about how such things should be regarded now. It settles nothing there. It only tells you plainly what was in us.

We looked for the raza - a sign tied to a hidden truth. Not a picture standing in for something else at a distance, the way a signpost points to a town but isn't the town. Bound to it. There was a moment. The water.

Before it comes teaching. We lay out the two ways before a person — a way of life and a way of death — and they walk toward the water knowing which one they have chosen. Write to Rome, though, and you find something else. When that church wrote to Corinth to settle a quarrel, the whole force of the letter fell on this: presbyters, plural, wrongly removed from an office they had held blamelessly and long.
